Internal engineering memo: local AI capacity versus better use of what we own

To: platform, ML, product, finance, security  
From: infrastructure review  
Re: whether to purchase additional local AI hardware now

The question is not whether the team needs more compute. It clearly does, eventually. The question is whether the next dollar should buy more accelerators, or should first be spent making the existing fleet do more useful work. My recommendation is to improve utilisation first, with a narrow, reversible purchase path if the evidence says we are genuinely capacity-bound.

The cost case is less simple than “new hardware is expensive.” Local hardware has a fixed cost, but it also carries hidden costs: power, cooling, rack space, maintenance, spare parts, staff time, and the opportunity cost of engineers spending weeks on provisioning instead of product. Buying more machines can look like a clean solution because it converts an operational problem into a procurement line item. That is seductive, but it can hide the real issue: many workloads are bursty, poorly batched, or running at low occupancy because scheduling, model selection, and routing are weak. If we buy capacity while those problems remain, we may simply add idle GPUs to an already inefficient estate.

Latency is the strongest argument for caution. Some workloads are latency-sensitive: interactive copilots, retrieval-augmented answers, and customer-facing assistants. Those need predictable response times, not just average throughput. But latency is often misdiagnosed. A slow system may be slow because of queueing, cold starts, oversized models, network hops, or serial dependencies, not because the GPU is undersized. Before purchasing, we should measure p50, p95, and p99 latency by workload, separate model inference from retrieval and orchestration, and identify whether the bottleneck is compute, memory bandwidth, storage, or application design. If p95 latency is dominated by queueing while utilization is low, the fix is scheduling and batching. If p95 is dominated by model size and memory pressure, targeted hardware may be justified.

Reliability matters as much as speed. More hardware increases the number of components that can fail, but it can also improve resilience if used for redundancy, isolation, and staged rollouts. The risk is that a larger estate without better observability becomes harder to operate. We should not add machines without adding dashboards, alerting, capacity forecasts, and runbooks. A small number of well-instrumented nodes can be more reliable than a larger fleet managed by tribal knowledge.

Opportunity cost is the part that is easy to underweight. Every week spent on procurement, installation, and validation is a week not spent on product, evaluation, and reliability work. That does not mean we should avoid hardware investment; it means we should be deliberate. The best use of the next quarter is likely to be a disciplined utilisation program: instrument utilization by workload, consolidate small jobs, batch offline inference, cache repeated prompts and embeddings, quantize or distill models where quality allows, route simple tasks to smaller models, and move non-urgent work to off-peak windows. These changes are reversible and relatively cheap.

Reversibility is another reason to start with utilisation. Software changes can be rolled back. A purchase is harder to undo. If we buy too much, the cost persists even if demand shifts. If we improve utilisation and still hit a hard ceiling, we can then buy with better evidence. That is not a reason to be passive; it is a reason to make the purchase decision later and with more confidence.

Uncertainty is real. Demand may grow faster than expected. Model quality requirements may force larger models. Security constraints may limit cloud fallback. If sustained p95 queueing, low utilization, and clear headroom in power and cooling all point the same way, then buying is right. But the current evidence does not justify a broad expansion.

So: do not approve a large new hardware purchase now. Approve a six-to-eight-week utilisation and observability effort, with explicit gates. If after that period utilization remains below roughly 60 to 70 percent while latency and queueing degrade, or if workloads cannot be batched without unacceptable quality loss, then proceed with a targeted purchase sized to the measured gap, not to the loudest request. Keep the purchase modular, avoid long-term commitments where possible, and revisit after the first quarter of improved operation. The goal is not to avoid hardware. It is to buy the right hardware, later, with evidence.

To: Engineering leadership
From: Platform and infrastructure working group
Re: Local AI hardware versus better utilisation of existing capacity

Recommendation up front: do not commit a large new hardware purchase yet. Spend the next two quarters improving utilisation, observability, scheduling, and workload shaping on the systems we already own, while placing a small, reversible expansion option in reserve. If utilisation gains and latency targets hold, revisit the purchase with measured demand rather than optimistic forecasts.

The case for buying more hardware is understandable. Local inference is attractive because it keeps data inside our boundary, reduces dependence on external services, and can give predictable latency for sensitive workloads. If demand is growing, more GPUs or accelerators may look like the simplest way to buy headroom. But the current evidence does not show that the bottleneck is raw capacity. It shows that capacity is unevenly used: some nodes are idle while others queue, some jobs run longer than they should, and some workloads are scheduled as if they were equally urgent. Buying more hardware into that pattern would mostly add idle silicon.

Cost is not only the sticker price. A new purchase carries depreciation, power, cooling, rack space, maintenance, staffing, and the opportunity cost of capital that could fund reliability work, developer tooling, or product features. It also carries a hidden cost: the temptation to treat hardware as the answer to every performance complaint. That is expensive in a way that does not appear on a purchase order. Utilisation work is cheaper and faster to reverse. If we misjudge the benefit, we can unwind a scheduling change, revise a quota, or cancel a lease. We cannot unwind a large capital commitment without regret.

Latency deserves careful treatment. Local hardware can improve tail latency when it removes network hops and external rate limits, but latency is also affected by batching, queueing, model size, memory pressure, and whether requests are being routed to the right tier. A larger fleet can reduce queueing, yet it can also increase fragmentation if workloads are not placed well. The right question is not “how many accelerators do we need?” but “which requests are latency-sensitive, which are throughput-oriented, and which should move to a different service class?” Some workloads may belong on local hardware; others may be better served by smaller models, cached responses, asynchronous processing, or carefully governed external inference.

Reliability is another reason to be cautious. More hardware increases the number of components, drivers, firmware versions, and failure modes. It can also make the system harder to reason about if ownership is unclear. Improving utilisation often improves reliability indirectly: clearer queues, better admission control, health checks, and backpressure reduce the chance that a single hot node becomes a silent failure. A modest expansion can help, but only after we know which failure modes are real. If the current pain is caused by overloaded nodes, more capacity helps. If it is caused by poor scheduling or unbounded retries, more capacity will not fix it.

Opportunity cost is the strongest argument for patience. The team is already stretched across product delivery, security review, and incident response. Spending time on a large procurement cycle would divert attention from the work that improves daily reliability. A phased approach lets us preserve optionality: we can buy a limited number of units, lease rather than own, or negotiate a capacity reservation while we gather evidence. That is not a refusal to invest; it is a way to invest with less irreversible risk.

Uncertainty remains. Demand may grow faster than expected, models may become larger, and local inference may become strategically important. If utilisation work shows that we are consistently at high utilization with stable latency, the case for expansion becomes much stronger. If we see that most requests are small, cacheable, or batchable, the case becomes weaker. We should therefore set explicit decision gates: utilization trend, p95 latency, queue depth, failure rate, and the share of workloads that cannot be moved or reduced.

My recommendation is a two-stage path. First, fund a focused utilisation program: instrumentation, workload classification, scheduling improvements, model routing, and capacity forecasting. Second, only after those results are in hand, approve a limited expansion, preferably leased or modular, sized to the measured gap rather than the hoped-for gap. This is not the cheapest path in the short term, but it is the most reversible and the most likely to produce durable value. We should be willing to buy more hardware if the evidence supports it; we should not buy it now because it feels like progress.
